e.t: Agab, also rendered Agav, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 2:46, identifying a person by name. The available form does not provide a separate descriptive meaning, so it is best understood as the personal name Agab or Agav. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

Adasan, also given as Athasan, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice: once in Joshua 15:37 and once in Nehemiah 7:54. The available information identifies the name but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to determine whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity in each passage.

“Brotherly” describes an action done with the warmth, care, or attitude appropriate between brothers. As an adverb, this word explains how someone acts rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 13:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense points to conduct marked by brotherly regard.

This Greek LXX noun means “singing praise”—an expressed offering of honor through song. It refers to praise voiced in worship, especially in passages connected with Israel’s worship and songs. The word occurs 67 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, with its largest concentration in Psalms. It can therefore describe praise as a spoken or sung act directed toward God. Its exact emphasis in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word is a proper name: “Alexandreus; Aleksanthrefs.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 3 Maccabees. The available information establishes its naming function, but not the person’s identity or role in either passage. Those details must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage context.

This adverb describes something done “in an ill-bred manner” or “rudely.” It points to behavior that is coarse, discourteous, or lacking proper politeness, rather than conduct marked by respect and good breeding. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 12:14. Its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its basic meaning remains a plain description of rude or uncivilized manner.

This Greek LXX noun means “repose” or “rest.” It refers to rest itself rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Job 3:23 and Isaiah 28:12. Both English renderings use “rest,” confirming this as its ordinary sense. The word’s precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea remains a state of rest or repose.

This noun means “bravery” or “manly virtue”—the quality of showing courage, strength, and noble character. It describes a valued kind of courage rather than merely physical power, pointing to a person’s readiness to act with firmness and honor. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, the word occurs eight times, including in Esther and 1–4 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains courageous, virtuous character.

This adjective means “of carbuncle,” describing something associated with or made of carbuncle. It identifies the material or nature of the thing being described rather than naming an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 1:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding description, but its central meaning remains a reference to carbuncle.

This word expresses opposition—something set against another—or substitution, where one thing stands instead of another. It commonly links people, objects, or actions by showing conflict, exchange, or replacement. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs 368 times, so its precise force depends on the sentence: it may point to resistance, a corresponding exchange, or one person or thing taking another’s place. Its basic ideas remain “against” and “instead of.”

This noun refers to a guardhouse or jail—a place where someone is confined or held under guard. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Jeremiah 36:26. The word itself identifies the confinement place, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular circumstances of its use. Its meaning is therefore concrete and straightforward: a secured place of detention, whether understood as a guardhouse or a jail.

This Greek verb means “stretch out” or “extend.” It describes directing or lengthening something outward, whether physically or in an action expressed by the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, each in a different verse, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided here. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on what is being extended and how the sentence uses the verb.

This Greek LXX noun means “breath” or “vapour,” referring to something breathed out or arising as a fleeting vapor. Its basic sense is physical and concrete rather than a technical description of a person or spiritual power. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Wisdom 11:18, so its wider scriptural range cannot be established from repeated uses. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Auaran is a proper name, referring to a person named Auaran or Avaran. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal designation. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Maccabees. The English rendering identifies the name as “Avaran,” while the lexical definition gives “Auaran; Avaran.” The precise person intended in either passage must be identified from the surrounding verse and narrative context.

This adjective describes someone or something exempt from tribute—that is, not required to provide a payment or levy. It expresses freedom from an imposed financial obligation rather than simply the absence of money. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 11:28, so its normal lexical sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The word functions as a description of exemption from tribute.

Bathesar, also rendered Vathisar, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament text, and it appears only once in this corpus, at Joshua 15:44. The available lexical information preserves the name but does not explain its personal or geographical identity, so its precise referent must be determined from the surrounding passage rather than from the name itself.

Bakcha, also rendered Vakkha, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 4:12. Because it functions as a personal or place name, its meaning is primarily identification: it points to the particular named person or location intended in that passage. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly whom or what Bakcha identifies there.

This rare Greek LXX noun appears to refer to something “in a sack?” The question mark signals that this meaning is uncertain rather than firmly established. It occurs only once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 1 Samuel 6:8. Without the verse text or surrounding context, its exact referent cannot be described more specifically. It is best understood as an uncertain noun connected with something being in a sack, while recognizing that the available wording does not permit a stronger conclusion.

This Greek LXX noun means “senator,” referring to a person who holds a recognized governing or deliberative office. It identifies a public official rather than an action, quality, or personal feeling. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in the book of Job. Its basic meaning remains the same wherever it appears, while the surrounding verse determines the particular role or situation being described.

This Greek LXX verb means “thunder”: it describes thunder sounding or occurring. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming the sound itself. The word identifies the action of thunder, while surrounding words determine who or what is said to thunder. It occurs nine times in the Greek LXX corpus, across passages from 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, Job, Psalms, and Sirach. Its precise force in any verse depends on that passage’s wording and context.

This noun describes nobleness of character—moral excellence marked by dignity, courage, and an admirable quality of person. It may be expressed by the simple idea of nobility, not merely by high social rank but by the worth and greatness of someone’s character. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in 2 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees. Its precise shade in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central meaning remains the commendable nobility or greatness found in a person’s character.

This adjective describes something with the tongue cut out. As an adjective, it qualifies a noun by identifying that physical condition. The wording is specific: it does not simply refer to the tongue, but describes one that has been cut. In the Greek LXX, this word occurs once, at Leviticus 22:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding text, but its basic meaning remains clear.

This verb means “remain”: to continue staying or continuing in existence rather than passing away or departing. It describes something that endures over time. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 20 times, including passages in Psalms, Sirach, Jeremiah, Wisdom, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what or whom the surrounding sentence says remains.

This noun means “dispersion” or “scattering”: the act or result of people or things being spread apart. It describes separation from a gathered place or group rather than unity or concentration. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Jeremiah and Ezekiel, though the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the particular situation each time. Its central idea remains the same: being scattered or dispersed rather than remaining together.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a “chariot-board”—the board or platform associated with a chariot. It names a physical part or surface rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, so its basic meaning remains a concrete transportation object. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central sense is the board or platform of a chariot.

This noun means “power” or “lordship”—the authority or rule held by someone who is able to govern or exercise might. In the Greek Old Testament, it can describe ruling power in human history and authority recognized in declarations about God. The word occurs 51 times across the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is broad: the power, dominion, or lordship by which someone acts or rules.

This Greek LXX verb means “get close” or “near.” It describes movement toward someone or something, or the state of coming into proximity. Because it is a verb, it normally expresses an action or change of position rather than naming a person or object. It occurs 144 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, making it a broadly used word for approaching or drawing near. Its exact force in a passage depends on what is being approached.

This Greek LXX verb means “overlook,” describing the act of looking over something or directing one’s sight across it. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 1 Samuel 13:18. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not provided here, the precise force of the verb in that sentence cannot be described further. Its basic lexical sense remains “overlook.”

This word describes something that one must admit or include. As an adjective, it characterizes what is required to be acknowledged or taken in. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Epistle of Jeremiah 1:56. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and paragraph, but its basic sense is an expression of something that must be admitted or included.

This Greek LXX noun refers to an outflow or a drain—something through which liquid runs away. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Ezekiel 40:39. The basic idea is a channel or means of removing flowing liquid, rather than the liquid itself. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the object being described.

This adjective means “of the fir,” describing something in relation to a fir tree. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at Ezekiel 27:5, so its use is rare in this corpus. Its role is to qualify a noun, identifying a connection with fir rather than naming the tree itself. The word may describe something made from fir or associated with it, while the surrounding verse determines the specific noun being described.

Elithenan is a personal name, not a common word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Septuagint, it appears three times, each time in genealogical material in 1 Chronicles. The name is preserved as “Elithenan” in the English rendering, and the available information does not provide a separate definition or interpretation of the name. Its precise reference is determined by the genealogy in each passage: 1 Chronicles 3:23, 1 Chronicles 3:24, and 1 Chronicles 7:8.

This word means “bonding.” It describes or names something that brings things together, holding them in connection. It can function as either an adjective or a noun, so it may identify a bonding quality or the thing that provides such a bond. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times across three verses, showing a specific but recurring use rather than a common term. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording.

gl: one of age; in the prime of manhood
d: one of age; in the prime of manhood

e.t: This noun refers to someone “one of age; in the prime of manhood”—an adult in the mature stage of life. It functions as a noun for a person who has reached maturity, rather than describing an action or quality. In the LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 18:9. The reference identifies where it appears, but the surrounding verse text is not included here.

This Greek LXX noun means “petition”—a formal request or appeal presented to someone who has authority to respond. It describes the request itself, rather than the person making it or the act of speaking. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in 3 Maccabees 6:40. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a petition brought forward for consideration. [p03:word:lxx:L704813:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L704813:occurrences] [p01:word:lxx:L704813:reference:0]

This verb means “draw out”: to pull something from within or bring it out. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Proverbs and once in Haggai, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided here. The word’s precise force in either passage depends on what is being drawn out, but its central idea remains bringing something outward from an inward or contained place.

This Greek LXX verb means “laid upon” or “imposed.” It describes something being placed on someone or something, or a burden, demand, or condition being put upon them. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming the object involved. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including passages from Exodus, Job, and the Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being placed or imposed and on the surrounding sentence.

This verb means “force on,” describing an action that presses forward or compels continued movement. It expresses what someone does rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice: once in Sirach and once in 1 Maccabees. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine who is forcing on and how the action functions in each passage.

This word is a verb that expresses an action or state. Its basic sense is “seven times”. It describes something happening or being done on seven occasions, or being repeated sevenfold. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twenty times, most often in Leviticus, where repeated actions are frequently specified. The word itself supplies a precise measure of repetition, while the surrounding sentence identifies what is repeated. Its earliest listed occurrence is Genesis 4:24, and its latest is 2 Maccabees 10:20.

gl: of solitude; living in a desert
d: of solitude; living in a desert

e.t: This adjective describes someone or something connected with solitude, especially life in a desert or uninhabited place. It can portray the condition of being apart from ordinary human settlement rather than simply naming a location. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both in Psalms, so its normal sense is focused and specific rather than broad. The exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains desert-like isolation or solitary living.

This adjective means “discoverable”: something that can be found, located, or brought to light. It describes a person or thing as available to be discovered rather than hidden beyond finding. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Judges 9:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains the possibility of being found or recognized.

gl: of good courage; stout of heart
d: of good courage; stout of heart

e.t: This adjective describes someone as “of good courage” or “stout of heart”—a person marked by bravery, confidence, and inner strength. It presents courage as a settled quality rather than merely a momentary feeling. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, the word occurs twice, once in Proverbs and once in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central sense remains a courageous, strong-hearted character.

This noun means the “fourth stomach of ruminating animals.” It refers to the fourth digestive chamber in animals that chew cud, such as cattle, sheep, and goats. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs twice, both within Malachi 2:3. The word itself identifies a specific bodily organ rather than expressing an action, quality, or spiritual condition. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the actual wording there.

This adjective describes someone who reveres God and lives with reverence toward him. “God-revering” and “reverential to God” express its central meaning. It points to a person’s orientation toward God rather than merely naming an outward religious action. In the LXX corpus, it occurs six times across Exodus, Job, and 4 Maccabees, showing its use in both Old Testament and later Greek Scripture. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “cure” or “minister to.” It describes providing care that helps someone, especially by restoring health or serving a need. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person or object. The word occurs 18 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used across several kinds of passages. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and situation.

This Greek LXX noun means “courage” or “boldness”—the quality of acting with confidence and resolve rather than fear or hesitation. It can describe a person’s daring attitude or the confident force shown in action. The word occurs 13 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages in Esther, Ezekiel, Wisdom, and the Maccabean books. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and situation.

Ieeth is a proper name, referring to a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 6:5. The available lexical information identifies the name simply as “Ieeth”; it does not provide an additional meaning or description. Its specific significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and genealogy.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Ieziēl” or “Iezil.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice: once in Joshua and once in 1 Chronicles. The name itself does not provide enough information to determine which person is intended in either passage; that identification depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its use is therefore chiefly as a personal designation within the biblical narrative.

Imana is a proper name, identifying a distinct named individual or thing rather than expressing a general quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 7:35. Since the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its precise referent must be established from that passage itself. The name is rendered consistently as “Imana.”

This noun means “charioteering,” referring to the activity or skill of driving and managing a chariot. It names an action connected with chariots and their movement, rather than a person or a specific vehicle. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Jeremiah 8:16 and Habakkuk 3:8. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine how the word functions in each passage, but its basic meaning remains the practice of chariot driving.

This is a proper name for an Ismaelite, a person belonging to the people called Ismaelites. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for people identified by this name rather than as a general description of an action or quality. The word occurs eight times in eight Old Testament verses, especially in Genesis, and also appears in Judges, 1 Chronicles, and Psalms. Its precise reference in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Kabeseel, also rendered Kavesil, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named place or person in the Greek Old Testament tradition, though the available lexical information does not specify which. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at 2 Samuel 23:20. Its precise referent is determined by the surrounding passage rather than by the name itself.

“Bit of reed” refers to a small piece of reed. As a noun, the word names a physical material rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 13 times, all in Exodus. Its recorded uses extend from Exodus 25:31 through Exodus 38:15, showing repeated use within that section of Exodus. The surrounding verse determines the precise object or part being described.

This noun means “caper-plant,” referring to the plant known for its small edible buds. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ecclesiastes 12:5. The word identifies a plant rather than an action, quality, or person. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical meaning is simply the caper-plant. The term is distinct to the Greek Old Testament wording represented here.

This word means “almond-like,” describing something that resembles an almond in some way. It is a Greek LXX word and occurs once, in Exodus 38:16. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s precise role in that passage cannot be described more specifically. Its central sense remains a comparison to an almond or something resembling one.

This verb means “grind down”: to wear something down by force or repeated action until it becomes smooth, diminished, or broken apart. It expresses an action rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 7:23. The surrounding verse determines whether the word’s force is understood literally or as a figurative description of overpowering and wearing down. Its basic idea remains the reduction of something through severe, sustained pressure.

This verb means to “cover with gold-leaf” or “gild.” It describes applying a layer of gold over an object, especially objects made for Israel’s worship. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 17 times in 16 verses, chiefly in Exodus and also in 2 Chronicles. The word focuses on the act of making something gold-covered, rather than simply describing its color or value. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on the object being gilded and the surrounding instructions.

This noun refers to a settler—someone who has come to live in a place, rather than merely passing through it. It describes a person viewed in relation to the community or land where that person resides. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word occurs three times: twice in the Old Testament and once in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is a person established as a resident in a place.

The word means “garden”: a cultivated place where plants, trees, or other growth are tended. It is a noun naming such a place rather than an action or quality. In this Greek Old Testament corpus, including its related deuterocanonical material, it occurs 36 times. Its basic meaning remains straightforward, while the surrounding passage determines the garden’s particular purpose or setting.

This Greek LXX noun means “strength”: the quality or power that makes someone or something strong. It names strength as a reality rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Psalms, and is rendered “strength” in each occurrence. Its precise force in either psalm depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning remains the possession or exercise of power and might.

This Greek LXX noun means “workman for hire” or “hired servant”—a person who works in return for payment. It identifies someone by an employment relationship rather than by family, rank, or personal name. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Job 2:9. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence must be understood from its context. Its basic sense remains a paid worker or servant, emphasizing service performed for compensation.

This noun means “witness”: a person who can testify to what was seen, heard, known, or established. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used especially in settings where testimony confirms a matter, supports an accusation, or establishes an agreement. The word occurs 58 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including passages concerning agreements, testimony, and legal judgment. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

Memmios is a proper name referring to a particular person. It does not describe a quality, action, or general idea; it identifies someone by name. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, Memmios occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 11:34. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, the name’s specific role in that sentence cannot be described further, but its basic meaning is the personal designation Memmios.

This verb means “change” or “transform.” As a verb, it describes an action in which something is made different from its former state or condition. The central idea is alteration: one thing becomes another in some relevant respect. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Wisdom 16:21. The word’s basic meaning remains the act of changing or transforming, while the surrounding sentence determines what is changed and how that change is understood. It should therefore be read as an action word, not as a name for a fixed object or person.

Mithradates is a proper name identifying a person, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. The Greek Old Testament glosses it as “Mithradatēs” and “Mithrathatis.” It appears twice in the Greek LXX, both times in Ezra: once in Ezra 1:8 and once in Ezra 4:7. Its meaning is therefore primarily its role as a personal name within these passages.

This noun means “perfumer,” a person who prepares fragrant oils, spices, or similar scented substances. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for someone whose work involves making or handling perfumes, including the preparation of sacred anointing oil and incense. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages in Exodus, Samuel, Chronicles, and Song of Songs. Its basic meaning remains focused on the occupation or craft of preparing perfumes rather than on a spiritual quality or symbolic idea.

Nabaal is a personal name, also rendered Navaal. It identifies an individual rather than expressing a general action, quality, object, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Joshua 19:15. Because the available passage context is not included here, the name itself does not provide further information about the person or the role associated with him. Its basic meaning is therefore the proper name Nabaal or Navaal.

Nard is the name of nard, functioning as a noun in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies what is being mentioned rather than describing an action, quality, or person. This word occurs three times in the Greek text of the Old Testament, all in Song of Songs: 1:12, 4:13, and 4:14. Its precise role in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic lexical meaning remains “nard.”

This adjective means “youthful” or “fresh,” describing someone or something marked by youth or freshness. It normally adds this quality to a person or thing rather than naming one by itself. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:8. Its precise force in that sentence depends on what it describes there, but the central idea remains youthfulness or freshness.

This word means “now” or “present”. It points to the current time or situation, marking what is happening at the moment being discussed. As an adverb, it modifies an action, statement, or circumstance by locating it in the present rather than the past or future. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 561 times, showing that it is a common word for directing attention to the immediate situation. Its basic meaning remains consistent, while the surrounding sentence determines exactly what present moment it identifies.

This Greek word means “back,” referring to the rear or upper surface of a person or thing. It is a noun, so it names that bodily or physical part rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 47 times, usually in passages involving a person’s body, the position of an object, or a physical direction. Its precise sense in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central meaning remains the back or rear side.

Oziza is a personal name, functioning as the designation of an individual rather than as a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezra 10:27. The available rendering preserves the name as “Oziza,” so its ordinary meaning is simply the person’s name; the name itself does not provide a further lexical description.

This noun refers to wine with a sharp, sour character, and it can also describe inexpensive wine. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears six times across five verses, including passages from Numbers, Ruth, Job, Psalms, and Proverbs. The central idea is a kind of wine identified by its taste or ordinary quality, rather than a person, action, or spiritual condition. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the basic meaning remains “sharp wine” or “cheap wine.”

Ousathi, also rendered Usathi, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 20:4. The available meaning information preserves the name itself but does not provide an additional definition or explanation of its origin. Its significance in that passage therefore comes from the surrounding account and the person identified by the name, not from a separate lexical idea attached to the name.

This adjective describes someone or something that is partly responsible for causing an outcome. It does not necessarily identify the sole or primary cause; rather, it points to a contributing role in what happened. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 11:19. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its basic sense is being in part the cause.

This word describes someone or something as five years old. It is an adjective that gives an exact age, rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Leviticus 27, where age is part of the wording used for valuation. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: the person or thing described has reached five years of age. The surrounding verse determines what is being assigned that age, but the word itself expresses only this specific age.

This verb means “slit and tear off,” describing the forceful act of cutting or splitting something and removing part of it. It presents a physical action rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Ezekiel, at Ezekiel 47:15 and 48:1. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly what is being slit and torn away in each occurrence.

This verb means “pitch,” describing the act of setting something in place. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it is used for an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs 34 times across 33 verses in this corpus, including passages from Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Judges, and 2 Samuel. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what is being pitched and the surrounding sentence.

This noun means “besieging” or “siege”: the surrounding of a city or stronghold to cut off its people and bring it under control. It names the act or condition of being pressed by such an assault, rather than the attackers themselves. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including references in Proverbs, Jeremiah, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word means “how often?” and functions as an adverb that asks about the frequency or repetition of an action. It focuses on the question of how many times something happens or is expected to happen, rather than describing the action itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including in 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Psalms, Sirach, and 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular sentence is determined by the surrounding wording, but its basic function remains a question about frequency.

“Cast forth; produce” is a verb for bringing something out, sending it forward, or causing it to come forth. It can describe an act of casting something outward or producing something that comes forth. The word appears eight times in this LXX corpus, across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic idea is used in more than one setting while retaining this movement or bringing-out sense. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This word means “front door”: the entrance or doorway at the front of a house or other building. It is a noun, so it names a physical place or structure rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs 23 times. Its basic sense is architectural: the doorway at the front or entrance area. The surrounding verse determines the particular building or setting being described.

This Greek verb means “send to”: it expresses directing or dispatching someone or something toward a person or destination. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what is being sent and where it is directed.

This word is a personal name, identifying Sabi, also given as Savi. It is not a descriptive term or action word; it functions as the name of a person in the Greek Old Testament text. This Greek LXX proper name refers to a place called Salem, also rendered Salim. It is a place-name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: twice in Genesis and once in Jeremiah. The exact significance of the place in any particular passage must be understood from that passage’s surrounding text, but the name itself identifies Salem or Salim.

This word is a proper name referring to Samuel, represented in the Greek Old Testament as “Samouēl” or “Samoil.” It identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Within the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, it occurs 144 times, appearing especially often in 1 Samuel. Its meaning is therefore its personal identification: the name Samuel.

Sēlōni is a proper name, rendered “Sēlōni; Siloni.” It identifies a person or family designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times, in Numbers, 1 Chronicles, and Nehemiah. The form is preserved as a name, so its precise reference in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and genealogical context.

“Overshadow” means to cast a shadow over something or someone, covering it from above or placing it under a shadow. As a verb, it describes an action or condition in which one thing covers, shelters, or darkens another. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, this word occurs 15 times, including passages from Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Job, and Baruch. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is doing the overshadowing and what is being covered.

This Greek LXX verb means “draw,” describing the action of pulling or moving something. It is a word of action rather than a name for a person, object, or quality. The word occurs 23 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, so its exact force depends on what is being drawn in each passage. Its recorded uses extend from Numbers through Sirach, showing that it serves as a normal action word across several kinds of biblical narrative and writing.

This Greek LXX verb means “make solid” or “solidify.” It describes an action that gives something firmness, stability, or strength rather than leaving it weak or unformed. As a verb, it expresses the act of making something firm, whether referring to a physical condition or a strengthened state. It occurs 49 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used across a broad range of passages. The surrounding verse determines what is being made firm in each occurrence.

This Greek LXX verb means “conjecture” or “join.” It can describe forming a conclusion or bringing things together, depending on how it functions in a sentence. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings represented here, so its basic sense is used across more than one setting. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and subject. It appears in passages ranging from 2 Chronicles and Isaiah to Sirach and 2 Maccabees.

This word means “companion”. It is a noun describing someone who accompanies another person or shares company with them. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Judges 11:37–38, showing a focused use rather than a broadly repeated term. The word identifies people connected through companionship, but the exact force in either verse must be understood from the surrounding passage. This verb means “weave together”: to join separate strands or pieces into one connected fabric. It describes combining parts so they hold together as a unified whole, rather than merely placing them side by side. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in Exodus. The surrounding verse determines exactly what materials or parts are being joined, but the central idea remains deliberate interlacing into one structure.

This verb means “let loose”: to release something or someone from restraint. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Amos 3:5. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the exact object being released must be understood from that passage. Sothele is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 7:21. The available wording preserves it as “Sothele,” so Scripture does not provide a broader ordinary meaning for the name itself. “Telēm; Telim” is a proper name, identifying a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs once, in Ezra 10:24. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the name itself establishes the person’s designation, but not further details about that individual or his role in the passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “district,” referring to a defined area or administrative region. It names a particular territorial division rather than a person, action, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 11:28. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is a recognized district or governed area.

This Greek LXX verb means to “head off” or “go,” describing movement from one place toward another. It presents departure or going as an action, rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Exodus and once in 4 Maccabees. The exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains the act of going or setting out.

“Stitch underneath” describes the action of sewing something beneath another piece or layer. It is a verb, so it names an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Sirach 50:1. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains the act of stitching underneath or sewing below. It should therefore be understood as a concrete sewing term, not as a general word for making or repairing.

Phoud, also given as Futh, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named person or people rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament: in Genesis, 1 Chronicles, and Isaiah. Because no verse text is provided here, its particular reference in each passage must be understood from the surrounding context. The lexical meaning is therefore the name itself: “Phoud” or “Futh.”

This verb means to guard or keep something, whether by watching over it, preserving it, or faithfully observing what is required. It can describe protecting a person or possession, maintaining something entrusted to one’s care, or keeping commands and appointed practices. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 448 times, showing broad use for both active protection and obedient observance. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what is being guarded or kept.

This Greek LXX verb means “yawn”: to open the mouth involuntarily, usually from tiredness, sleepiness, or weariness. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or lasting condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 2:8. The surrounding verse is needed to determine the precise force of the action in that passage, but the word itself plainly expresses yawning. This noun means “need”: a lack, requirement, or necessity that calls for something to meet it. It can describe what a person or situation requires, whether that need concerns practical provision or another necessary response. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 49 times, showing a recurring word for matters that are necessary or required. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “juice,” referring to the liquid expressed from a plant, fruit, or other substance. It is a noun, so it names the liquid itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 6:25. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning is simply juice.

This noun means “molten image”: an image formed from material melted into shape. It refers to a physical representation or idol rather than to the act of melting itself. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs five times, in passages from Deuteronomy, 2 Kings, Jeremiah, Hosea, and Habakkuk. Its basic sense remains focused on an image made through a molten process, while the surrounding passage determines what is said about that image.
